docs.title: Discover methods
docs.text: These calls show which methods fit your data and your task. They need no environments, GPU or data.

docs.title: The four integration categories
docs.text:
Pick the category that matches your experimental design and pass it as category= first. A method written for one design cannot take data from another.

Category Design Typical modalities vertical Several modalities measured in the same cells RNA+ADT, RNA+ATAC, RNA+ADT+ATAC diagonal Modalities measured in different cells, bridged by shared features RNA batch + ATAC batch mosaic Several batches with different modalities, linked by a batch that measures two of them mixed, partially paired cross Several batches, each with every modality RNA+ADT, RNA+ATAC, ADT+ATAC, RNA+ADT+ATAC

Several samples of 10x Multiome (RNA+ATAC) belong in vertical: one folder with all cells. To score batch mixing, pass each cell's sample as batch= to run or evaluate.

docs.title: Filter by what your data has
docs.text:
find_methods lists the methods, all of them without a filter. Its filters are what your data has: the category, the modalities you measured, how your ATAC is encoded, and whether you have cell-type labels.

import multibench as mtb

mtb.find_methods()                       # all methods
mtb.find_methods(category="vertical")    # paired-design methods only

Each method reads ATAC either as peaks or as gene activity. Give each method the representation it reads: atac_peak or atac_gas in modalities= keeps the methods that read yours.

# unpaired RNA and ATAC batches, no cell-type labels
mtb.find_methods(category="diagonal", modalities=["rna", "atac"],
                 needs_labels=False)
# ['SCALEX', 'Seurat_v5', 'VIPCCA', 'Portal', ...]

mtb.find_methods(category="diagonal", modalities=["atac_peak"])   # ATAC as peaks
Details

A method matches when one of its variants meets all the filters together. A variant is the version of a method for one category and one set of inputs. None, the default, turns a filter off.

modalities= keeps the variants that take every listed type, so ["rna"] is broad and ["rna", "atac"] stricter. "atac" matches any ATAC input, and protein means adt.

The other ATAC tokens select by what the method reads. "gas", "gene_activity" and "atac_gas" keep the methods that read gene activity. "peak" and "atac_peak" keep those that read peaks, including moETM, scMM and iPOLNG, whose input is named atac_gas. Naming both representations keeps MultiMAP and Seurat_v3, which read both files.

mtb.scan and run use the same tokens. They keep a row only when its modalities are exactly the listed ones, so scMoMaT's rna+adt+atac row is not kept for ["rna", "atac"]. A representation token keeps every row whose method reads it, so "atac_peak" also keeps MultiMAP and Seurat_v3.

needs_labels is judged per variant. method_info(m)["needs_labels"] is True when any variant needs labels.

An unknown token raises ValueError listing the valid values. A bare string such as modalities="rna" raises TypeError.

docs.title: My ATAC is peaks only
docs.text:
Most diagonal methods read gene activity. With a peak matrix alone, check which methods can run:

  • GLUE runs on peaks. It reads peak names such as chr1:100-200, and a run rewrites chr1_100_200 or chr1-100-200 into that form. It also needs the GENCODE annotation file. See Run a method.
  • Seurat_v5 needs a third dataset: a paired bridge with RNA and ATAC from the same cells. The package passes your RNA and ATAC files as that bridge, so it cannot run on unpaired data here.
  • MultiMAP and Seurat_v3 also need gene activity for the same ATAC cells.
  • The other ten need gene activity instead of peaks, for the ATAC cells of atac_peak.h5. Make it outside the package, for example with Signac GeneActivity, read it into an AnnData gas, and write it into the folder with mtb.io.export_dataset(gas, "data/X", rna=None, atac="X", atac_kind="gene_activity", category="diagonal").

mtb.scan then shows which methods have their files.

Details

mtb.scan compares the cells of atac_gas.h5 with those of atac_peak.h5. Other cells, or the same cells in another order, fail the file check. Barcodes that differ only in a suffix such as -1 or -2 count as the same cell.

export_dataset writes the rows in the cell order of the folder's atac_peak.h5, which atac_cty.csv follows, and refuses other cells.

docs.title: Inspect a single method
docs.text:
method_info returns what the package knows about one method.

info = mtb.method_info("SCALEX")
info["env"], info["atac"], info["needs_labels"]
# ('scmb_torch', 'gene_activity', False)
info["supports"]    # one entry per variant: category, modalities, labels, ...
info["runtime"]     # {'measured_sec': 301, 'tier': 'medium', 'worst_sec': 2233, ...}
Details

measured_sec is the package's own run on the full stored dataset, and tier (fast to very_slow) follows it. worst_sec, the longest of runtime["observed"], sets run(timeout=...). On a CPU, training methods take much longer than these times.

info["setup_hint"] names what a method needs before its first run, such as GLUE's annotation file. setup_hint is empty for most methods. mtb.params_for(method, category, modalities) lists what run(params=...) can change and what the script fixes.

Unknown method ids raise KeyError. Every function takes a method id in any case, and the paper's spellings such as MOFA+.

The keys of method_info are listed in its reference entry. gpu says how a method uses an NVIDIA GPU: required, used when present, not used or unknown. cpu_params holds the flags that turn CUDA off, which a run adds on a computer without a GPU.

docs.title: Rank from stored results
docs.text:
rank ranks a category's methods by their stored results, in the order of the figures.

mtb.rank("vertical", modalities=["rna", "adt"])
#   method  grand_score  needs_labels  runtime_tier  worst_sec  env
mtb.rank("diagonal", modalities=["atac_peak"])   # only methods that read peaks
mtb.rank("vertical", methods=mtb.find_methods("vertical", needs_labels=False))

grand_score compares a category's methods with each other: it is a rank, not a quality score. How it evaluates says how it is computed.

The stored results cover one dataset per category: for vertical, D11 (RNA + ADT). Read the ranking as a hint. The full benchmark ranking is in the interactive explorer and in Fig. 6 of the paper. Methods with needs_labels=True train on your cell types, so compare them only with each other.

Details

The Seurat_v5 script reads its bridge as two extra files. Its stored diagonal scores come from runs with a separate paired bridge dataset. They do not mean that it runs on your unpaired folder.

To rank your own method alongside, pass long_df=pd.concat([mtb.load_results(category), mine]).

Methods that fit the category but have no stored results are listed last, with grand_score NaN. modalities= naming a modality that no ranked dataset measured raises.

modalities= follows the find_methods rule above. It only shortens the list, so a filtered list can start below 1 and end above 0.

metrics= picks the metric family. The default ranks on every metric present, as the figures do. needs_labels follows the category's variants.

docs.title: The full benchmark catalog
docs.text:
mtb.catalog returns the dataset and metric tables as DataFrames.

mtb.catalog.datasets()    # the fetchable datasets: category, has_results
mtb.catalog.metrics()     # each metric with its family and what it measures
Details

The rows are the demo datasets, which mtb.data.fetch downloads. has_results marks the datasets with stored results.

Next: run a chosen method in Run a method, score its output in Score an embedding, and compare methods in Load and plot results.

docs.title: Score an embedding
docs.text:
mtb.evaluate scores an embedding against cell-type labels with the paper's metrics and returns them as a long table. An embedding is a table with one row per cell, like adata.obsm["X_pca"].

Summary

import scanpy as sc
import multibench as mtb

mtb.data.fetch("D11")
mtb.data.write_example("D11")     # my_file.h5ad: cell types in obs["celltype"]
adata = sc.read_h5ad("my_file.h5ad")
sc.pp.normalize_total(adata)
sc.pp.log1p(adata)
sc.pp.pca(adata)                  # the embedding to score: adata.obsm["X_pca"]
scores = mtb.evaluate(adata, labels="celltype", obsm="X_pca", method="PCA",
                      category="vertical", metrics="clustering")
print(scores)

docs.title: Choose the metrics
docs.text:
metrics= takes a family ("clustering", "batch", "classification", "all"), a metric code, or a list of codes and families. The default computes every metric your inputs allow except kBET.

mtb.evaluate(adata, labels="celltype", obsm="X_pca", metrics="cLISI")
mtb.evaluate(adata, labels="celltype", obsm="X_pca", metrics=["ARI", "NMI"])

The protocol is the paper's. ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW and iF1 score Leiden clusters searched to the number of cell types. ARI_batch and NMI_batch score Leiden clusters searched to the number of batches.

Details

The search bisects the Leiden resolution on [0, 3] for at most 30 steps until the clustering has the number of clusters wanted. When no step gets there, the last step's clusters are scored. The clusters come from scanpy's default 15-neighbour graph of the embedding, or of its first 50 principal components when it is wider, as in the paper. cLISI, iLISI and GC use the 15-neighbour graph of the whole embedding.

A selection without the seven metrics above skips the search, such as metrics="cLISI".

kBET is computed only when a list names it, and can take hours on large datasets.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Pass the embedding and one cell-type label per cell, in the embedding's row order. Both can be paths or in-memory objects. The reference lists the accepted forms.

# embedding and labels in one AnnData
mtb.evaluate(adata, labels="celltype", obsm="X_pca")

A column is named with or without obs:, so labels="obs:celltype" is the same. To score a method's output, use evaluate(dataset=, category=, method=) and no labels=: the embedding.h5 that run writes names its cells, and evaluate matches the label files to them.

A missing label is not a cell type: evaluate raises when a label is missing, and so does a missing batch. Score the labelled cells, as adata[adata.obs["celltype"].notna()].

Details

The labels of a dataset folder, in its cell order:

import pandas as pd
folder = mtb.data.fetch("D52mini")
order = {"rna": 0, "adt": 1, "atac": 2}
files = sorted(folder.glob("*cty*.csv"),
               key=lambda f: (order.get(f.stem.split("_")[0], -1), len(f.stem), f.stem))
labels = pd.concat([pd.read_csv(f).iloc[:, 0] for f in files]).to_numpy()

They follow the folder's cells as mtb.io.read reads them: RNA before ADT before ATAC, batches by number.

labels takes a CSV path with a header row (column x, or the only column), a list of CSV paths stacked in that order, a 1-D array or Series, or the name of an .obs column. batch takes the same forms.

With an AnnData, labels and batch can name .obs columns, and obsm= names the embedding. A MuData works the same way, with the joint embedding in its .obsm, and "rna:celltype" names a column of one modality.

A label is missing when it is NaN, None, blank text, or text that a label file reads as missing, such as NA, nan or null.

When the output has cell ids, the ids decide. An AnnData, an .h5ad file, a DataFrame indexed by cell id and a CSV embedding whose first column holds the barcodes have them. A Series indexed by cell id, or a CSV whose first column holds the cell ids, is then aligned by id. Ids of other cells are left out. Where barcodes repeat across a dataset's label files, a cell id is the label file and the barcode, as cty2:AAAC..., the way res.embedding(m) names cells.

A label file without cell ids in a dataset folder takes the cell ids of the matrix next to it. Any other file or Series without cell ids is refused: add the barcodes, or pass .to_numpy() to match by position.

A bare array has no cell ids. A Series or a CSV is then matched by position, with a warning when it holds cell ids. Plain arrays and lists are always matched by position.

A run's embedding.h5 holds the name of each cell (the dataset barcodes), so dataset= matches the label files to its cells whatever method= says. In a run folder written before 0.4.0, the run's record names the method that made the file. For an embedding without cell names, dataset= reads the cell order of method= when it names a package method, also as method="StabMap (this run)", else the folder's order: numbered files ascending, and rna before adt before atac. StabMap puts its reference batch first, which is cty3 on D52. Without category=, a benchmark dataset gives it. On a folder of your own, a package method needs it. A list of label files is stacked in the order given.

docs.title: Batch metrics
docs.text:
Batch metrics also need one batch per cell. Pass batch=, or dataset= of a multi-batch dataset folder without labels: each of its label files is then a batch. Give the category and the method too, so the files follow the rows of the method's output. A wrong order gives wrong scores without an error.

mtb.data.fetch("D52mini")
mtb.data.write_example("D52mini", "d52")   # d52/my_file.h5ad: donors in obs["batch"]
cross = sc.read_h5ad("d52/my_file.h5ad")
sc.pp.normalize_total(cross)
sc.pp.log1p(cross)
sc.pp.pca(cross)
mtb.evaluate(cross, labels="celltype", batch="batch", obsm="X_pca", metrics="all")
Details

ARI_batch and NMI_batch are 1 minus the absolute ARI and NMI between the batch clusters and the batches, so higher means better mixed batches.

Without batch=, run uses each cell's label file as its batch, so batches inside one file, such as donors, are not scored. Pass batch= to run, or re-score saved outputs with the real batch vector, mtb.load_run("out/").rescore(batch=...). No method is re-run.

docs.title: Classification metrics
docs.text:
With two or more batches, evaluate also predicts each cell's type from another batch and scores the predictions: OCA, ACA, Spec, Sens and F1. The default adds them unless category="vertical".

mtb.evaluate(cross, labels="celltype", batch="batch", obsm="X_pca",
             metrics="classification")
Details

Each batch in turn is the reference that a small neural network learns from, as in the paper. The scores are the mean over the references, as the paper reports them.

They need the method's embedding. A graph method has none, and run leaves them out for it. Where they cannot be computed, metrics="classification" raises. "all" gives NaN with a warning, and so does the default, except on data in one batch, where it leaves them out.

For vertical data in several batches, ask for them with metrics="classification".

docs.title: The result
docs.text:
evaluate returns the long table: one row per metric, with the columns metric, value, method, dataset, category, source and scored_with. method=, dataset= and category= fill their columns, and source reads user. A metric that cannot run on your machine is NaN, with a warning.

scores.to_csv("mine.csv", index=False)
scores.pivot(index="method", columns="metric", values="value")

Add your own method concatenates it with the stored results.

docs.title: What each metric measures
docs.text:
mtb.catalog.metrics() returns this table. The details below give the exact computation.

Metric Family Description ARI clustering Adjusted Rand Index: how well the Leiden clusters, one per cell type, match the cell-type labels. About 0 = random, 1 = identical, higher = better. NMI clustering Normalized Mutual Information: how much the Leiden clusters, one per cell type, tell about the cell-type labels. 0-1, higher = better. ASW clustering Average silhouette width: how well the Leiden clusters, one per cell type, separate from each other on the embedding. Rescaled to 0-1, higher = better. iASW clustering Isolated-label silhouette: each cell's silhouette (distance to the nearest other Leiden cluster), averaged per cluster and then over the clusters. Every cluster is treated as an isolated label, where scib's default counts only labels found in few batches. 0-1, higher = better. iF1 clustering Isolated-label F1: how well one Leiden cluster captures each cell type, the best F1 of one cluster (one cluster per cell type), averaged over the cell types. Every cell type is treated as an isolated label, where scib's default counts only types found in few batches. 0-1, higher = better. cLISI clustering Cell-type LISI: how much each cell's neighbours share its cell type on the embedding, the median over cells, scaled to 0-1, higher = better. ASW_batch batch Batch silhouette: how well the batches mix within each cell type, 1 minus the absolute batch silhouette within each cell type, averaged over the cell types. 0-1, higher = better. ARI_batch batch Batch ARI: how little the Leiden clusters, one per batch, match the batches, 1 minus their absolute Adjusted Rand Index. 0-1, higher = better. NMI_batch batch Batch NMI: how little the Leiden clusters, one per batch, tell about the batches, 1 minus their Normalized Mutual Information. 0-1, higher = better. GC batch Graph connectivity: how much of each cell type stays in one connected group of neighbours, the share of its cells in the largest connected part of its neighbour graph, averaged over the cell types. 0-1, higher = better. iLISI batch Integration LISI: how many batches appear among each cell's neighbours on the embedding, the median over cells, scaled to 0-1, higher = better. kBET batch k-nearest-neighbour batch effect test: how often a neighbourhood holds the overall batch mix, 1 minus the rate at which the test rejects that mix, averaged over the cell types. 0-1, higher = better. OCA classification Overall classification accuracy: the fraction of query cells predicted correctly. 0-1, higher = better. ACA classification Average classification accuracy: the fraction of each cell type predicted correctly, averaged over the cell types. 0-1, higher = better. Spec classification Specificity, averaged over the cell types. 0-1, higher = better. Sens classification Sensitivity, averaged over the cell types. 0-1, higher = better. F1 classification F1-score, averaged over the cell types. 0-1, higher = better. Details

cLISI and iLISI need scib's compiled LISI helper. Where the binary scib ships cannot run, evaluate rebuilds it once if a C++ compiler (g++, c++ or clang++) is on PATH. Otherwise the warning prints the build command.

kBET needs R through rpy2. Otherwise kBET is NaN.

Each metric is a scib function on the embedding. The package needs scib 1.1 or newer, and attrs["scib_version"] records the version.

code       scib function         settings the table above does not give
ARI, NMI   ari, nmi
ASW        silhouette
iASW       isolated_labels_asw   iso_threshold = number of batches + 1
iF1        isolated_labels_f1    iso_threshold = number of batches + 1
cLISI      clisi_graph           90 nearest cells by path on the
                                 15-neighbour graph
ASW_batch  silhouette_batch
ARI_batch  ari
NMI_batch  nmi
GC         graph_connectivity    the 15-neighbour graph
iLISI      ilisi_graph           as cLISI, for the batches
kBET       kBET

cLISI and iLISI take the median m of the per-cell scores and scale it: cLISI = (L - m)/(L - 1) and iLISI = (m - 1)/(B - 1), with L cell types and B batches.

docs.title: Look at an embedding
docs.text:
res.embedding(method) returns a method's embedding as an AnnData, with the cell types in obs["label"]. Three scanpy lines draw its UMAP:

import scanpy as sc

e = res.embedding("Matilda")          # or mtb.load_run("out/").embedding("Matilda")
sc.pp.neighbors(e, use_rep="X_emb"); sc.tl.umap(e); sc.pl.umap(e, color="label")

When the dataset folder was written from your AnnData, the cells' names are its obs_names, and one line puts the embedding into it: adata.obsm["X_Matilda"] = e[adata.obs_names].obsm["X_emb"].

docs.title: Are my numbers comparable?
docs.text:
Score a method's output with the dataset's own labels, in the method's cell order: mtb.evaluate(embedding, dataset=..., category=..., method=...).

Scores of your runs can differ a little from the stored ones: some methods, such as sciPENN and VIMCCA, give a slightly different embedding on each run. The Leiden-based and classification scores of the same embedding also depend on the cells' order. Above 4,096 cells, the same embedding also scores a few hundredths differently on another computer, because the neighbours are approximate.

Details

The scored_with column records how the scores were computed: the Leiden backend, where the clusters came from and the multibench version, such as leidenalg/search/0.4.0.

docs.title: Mosaic integration: [RNA, RNA + ADT, ADT]¶
docs.text:
Mosaic integration combines batches that share only some modalities. This tutorial is for an RNA batch, an RNA + ADT batch and an ADT batch. It runs StabMap and scMoMaT on D38mini, 6,000 cells of the benchmark dataset D38, and then on data in your own format.

Methods run on Linux. On macOS or Windows, open this notebook in Colab: sections 1 to 4 take about 11 minutes there.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text: pip may then print a note about restarting the kernel: no restart is needed, because the pins keep the numpy and pandas already installed.

docs.title: 2. Download the data and the environments¶
docs.text: mtb.data.fetch downloads D38mini (2 MB) once. mtb.env.install downloads the environments for StabMap and scMoMaT. The download is 1.8 GB on a computer without a GPU and 5.4 GB on one with a GPU.

docs.title: 3. Run the methods¶
docs.text:
run runs each method on D38mini and scores its output. The clustering metrics score how well the embedding's clusters and neighbourhoods match the cell types, and how separate the clusters are. The batch metrics measure how well the batches mix. The classification scores measure how well the cell types learned on one batch are predicted in the other batches. scMoMaT writes a graph: run scores its 2-D UMAP, with no classification scores. Higher is better for every metric.

Details

params={"Method": {"key": value}} sets a method's parameters, and mtb.params_for lists them.

mtb.load_run("out/D38mini") reloads these results later.

docs.title: 4. Plot¶
docs.text:
res.plot() draws the scores as a bubble table. Circle size ranks the rows within each column and colour shows the value scaled per column, so a small gap can look large. res.summary has the values.

Details

Metrics are grouped by family: blue for clustering, green for batch correction, pink for classification. Each family starts with an Overall bar: each row's mean rank over the family's metrics, scaled so that the lowest gets the shortest bar.

A column with fewer than two different values is drawn grey. A figure of one method is grey everywhere.

docs.title: 5. Your own data¶
docs.text:
Your data needs raw counts, with one .h5ad file per batch and modality and a cell type for each cell. Number the batches as below: RNA, then RNA + ADT, then ADT.

Every RNA file needs the same gene names and every ADT file the same protein names, in the same order. scMoMaT matches the features of two batches by position, and the check does not compare their names across batches.

Recipes cover a 10x .h5 file, labels in a CSV file and no labels.

Details: export

The folder layout lists the batch patterns and the methods that accept each one.

When the ADT file also holds a matrix in obsm under a name that does not start with X_, export_dataset asks which one is the protein matrix. X_umap and X_pca are left alone.

This tutorial is for an RNA + ADT batch, an RNA + ATAC batch and an RNA batch, so every batch holds RNA. It runs StabMap and UINMF on D46mini, 4,500 cells of the benchmark dataset D46, and then on data in your own format.

docs.title: 3. Run the methods¶

mtb.load_run("out/D46mini") reloads these results later.

Details

A column with fewer than two different values is drawn grey. A figure of one method is grey everywhere.

This tutorial is for an RNA + ADT batch, an RNA + ATAC batch and an ADT batch, so no modality is in every batch. It runs StabMap and scMoMaT on D49mini, 4,500 cells of the benchmark dataset D49, and then on data in your own format.

Methods run on Linux. On macOS or Windows, open this notebook in Colab: sections 1 to 4 take about 11 minutes there.

docs.title: Load and plot results
docs.text:
mtb.load_results reads the stored results, the package's own runs of its methods, into one long table. mtb.plot.bubble draws the paper's bubble table from it.

Summary

import multibench as mtb

df = mtb.load_results("vertical", dataset="D11")
fig = mtb.plot.bubble(df, metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "cLISI"],
                      title="Vertical integration, D11", save="d11.pdf")

docs.title: Step 1: Load a results table
docs.text:
load_results returns a long table: one row per method, dataset and metric. Every plotting function takes this table.

import multibench as mtb

df = mtb.load_results(
    "vertical",            # vertical | diagonal | mosaic | cross
    dataset="D11",         # a list for several; omit for all
)
df.head()
Details

methods= and metrics= narrow the table and accept aliases, such as "mofa+" for MOFA2. metrics= takes the same values as in evaluate.

The stored results cover these datasets:

Category datasets vertical D11 diagonal D28 mosaic D45 cross D52

The stored results have no kBET scores.

docs.title: Step 2: Draw the bubble table
docs.text:
mtb.plot.bubble draws one row per method, best on top, and one column per metric. It returns a Matplotlib Figure.

fig = mtb.plot.bubble(
    df,
    metrics=["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "cLISI"],   # column order within each family
    title="Vertical integration, D11",
    save="d11_bubble.pdf",
)
Details

The reference lists every option. These are used most often:

  • methods=[...] keeps only these methods, before ranking.
  • metrics="clustering" draws one family.

docs.title: Reading the figure
docs.text:
Circle size shows the rank within a column. A bigger circle is better. Fill colour is scaled within each column of this figure. The lightest fill is the lowest value in that column. Each metric family starts with an Overall bar, and rows are in the order of mtb.rank.

Details

Blue columns are the clustering family, green columns the batch-correction metrics, and pink columns the classification metrics.

A grey column holds the same value in every row. A figure with one method is grey in every column. A warning names the grey columns.

A dash marks a metric not computed for that method. Its Overall averages the metrics it has.

The chips give each method's language, Py or R. Matilda (this run) has Matilda's. ? marks a name the package does not know, such as your own method.

docs.title: Several datasets
docs.text:
mtb.plot.bar ranks the methods within each dataset and draws one bar per method with its score across the datasets, in the colour of the metrics= family: "clustering", "batch" or "classification". mtb.rank(category, long_df=df, metrics="clustering") gives the same scores, in the same order, as a table.

import pandas as pd

# res_a, res_b: mtb.run on two dataset folders
df = pd.concat([res_a.long, res_b.long])
fig = mtb.plot.bar(df, metrics="clustering", title="Two datasets")
mtb.rank("vertical", long_df=df, metrics="clustering")
Details

The stored results hold one dataset per category: a bar chart of one of them draws one bar per method.

plot.bubble of several datasets averages each method's values per column. Each row label shows the method's dataset, or how many datasets it averages (Matilda · 2 ds). A warning says so. When the datasets share no method, plot each dataset on its own.

A method missing from a dataset is left out there: its score is the mean over the datasets it was scored on. A warning lists these methods, and methods= keeps the ones scored on every dataset.

docs.title: Add your own method
docs.text:
Score your run with mtb.evaluate and concatenate it with the stored results. Are my numbers comparable? says what to expect.

d11_panel.py
import pandas as pd
import multibench as mtb

bench = mtb.load_results("vertical", dataset="D11")
# emb: your embedding, cells x dims, in the order of the D11 labels
mine = mtb.evaluate(emb, dataset="D11", category="vertical", method="MyMethod")

both = pd.concat([bench, mine])
metrics = ["ARI", "NMI", "ASW", "cLISI"]
fig = mtb.plot.bubble(both, metrics=metrics,
                      title="Vertical integration, D11 + MyMethod",
                      save="d11_vertical.pdf")
ranks = mtb.rank("vertical", long_df=both, metrics=metrics)
print(list(ranks.method).index("MyMethod") + 1)   # its row in the figure
Details

Give your run a name the stored results do not use, such as "Matilda (this run)" for a run of a package method. It reads Matilda's cell order. Duplicate (method, dataset, metric) rows raise instead of being averaged.

To put your embedding next to your runs on your own folder, pass that folder as dataset=, such as dataset="mydata/MYCITE".

The stored methods set the scale of the overall score, so your rows can score above 1 or below 0.

docs.title: Try it with a PCA of D11
docs.text:
To try the recipe without a method of your own, use a PCA of D11's RNA as emb. Put these lines above bench = ... in d11_panel.py, then run the script.

import scanpy as sc

d = mtb.data.fetch("D11")
rna = mtb.io.read(d / "rna.h5")
sc.pp.normalize_total(rna)
sc.pp.log1p(rna)
sc.pp.highly_variable_genes(rna, n_top_genes=2000)
sc.pp.pca(rna)
emb = rna.obsm["X_pca"]

docs.title: Run a method
docs.text:
mtb.run runs the methods you name on a dataset folder, each in its own environment, scores each output and saves the results. methods=["SCALEX"] runs one method.

Methods run on Linux, and on Windows for the methods with a Windows environment. SCALEX, the example of this page, runs on Linux only. On macOS, mtb.scan(dataset, category, command=True) returns the plan with each command. Run the call itself on a Linux machine.

Summary

import multibench as mtb

mtb.data.fetch("D28")                  # 137 MB; skipped when already present
res = mtb.run("D28", "diagonal", methods=["SCALEX"], out_dir="runs/")
res.summary                            # status, run time and every score
emb = res.embedding("SCALEX")          # AnnData: obsm["X_emb"], 11014 x 10
Details

run finds the version of the method that fits the category and the files of the folder. It converts the files if needed, runs the method script in <out_dir>/<method>_<dataset>/ and scores its output.

mtb.scan creates no files: with command=True its command column holds each command, with <out_dir> for the output folder.

Some commands read a file that run writes first under <out_dir>/<method>_<dataset>/inputs/, such as a converted AnnData, the renamed peak file of GLUE and Seurat_v3, or the links to the data files of scMM, scMVP and scJoint. The caveat column of scan says so. Call mtb.run in the job for those methods, not the command alone.

docs.title: Install the method's environment
docs.text:
Install the method's environment before its first run. mtb.env.install(["SCALEX"], dry_run=True) lists what is installed and what is missing, with the download sizes.

mtb.method_info("SCALEX")["env"]                # 'scmb_torch'
mtb.env.install(["SCALEX"])
Details

A missing environment marks the method not runnable in mtb.scan, and run skips it. On macOS the reason says that methods run only on Linux.

GLUE reads the GENCODE v43 human annotation, which its first run downloads, and MIRA a logger.py, which the package puts next to its script. GLUE runs its human script only, so mouse data does not run through the package. mtb.method_info(m)["setup_hint"] holds these notes, and the caveat column of scan lists them.

docs.title: What run returns
docs.text:
res is a RunResult. res.summary has one row per method: its status, run time and scores, and its reason column says why a method failed or was skipped. res.embedding(method) returns the method's embedding as an AnnData, in the method's cell order: obsm["X_emb"]. Its obs holds each cell's label, and its batch when the run had more than one batch: the label file of each cell, or the batch= of run. The cell names are the barcodes of the dataset files. Where two files share a barcode, each name starts with its label file, such as cty2:AAACCTGAG....

res.summary[res.summary.status != "scored"]   # empty when every method scored
emb = res.embedding("SCALEX")
emb.obs.head()                     # label, and batch, per cell
res.long                           # the scores, as the long table
res = mtb.load_run("runs/")        # the same result, later

run also writes the cell names into each embedding.h5, as the dataset barcodes, so mtb.evaluate and mtb.io.read find each cell of the file by its name.

Details

res.records holds one dict per method, with the keys mtb.RunResult lists. Five methods put the cells in another order than RNA before ATAC and cty1, cty2, .... uniPort and Seurat_v5 put the ATAC cells first. StabMap puts its reference batch first, in cross and in the mosaic patterns that start with an RNA-only batch. SMILE and MultiVI in mosaic use their own batch order. embedding(method) and mtb.evaluate(..., dataset=, method=) follow that order.

method_info(m)["supports"] gives each variant's output_kind, embedding or graph. Embedding metrics such as ASW do not apply to a graph. run scores scMoMaT through the UMAP embedding that scMoMaT also writes. MIRA and Seurat_WNN get the status ran, and the reason says that they write a graph.

res.rescore(batch=..., labels=..., metrics=...).save() scores the saved outputs again and writes the new scores. metrics= replaces those scores and keeps the others. No method runs again.

docs.title: Set a method's parameters
docs.text:
Every method takes parameters. mtb.params_for(method, category, modalities) lists them with their defaults, which are the paper's values. A default of None leaves the setting to the method's library. run(params={method: {name: value}}) sets them. For several values of one parameter, loop over run, one out_dir per value, and name each run's rows:

import pandas as pd

p = mtb.params_for("scJoint", "diagonal")
p["tunable"]["epochs_stage1"]          # {'default': 20, 'type': 'int'}

runs = []
for v in (10, 30, 50):
    r = mtb.run("D28", "diagonal", methods=["scJoint"], out_dir=f"runs/e{v}",
                params={"scJoint": {"epochs_stage1": v}})
    runs.append(r.long.assign(method=f"scJoint epochs={v}"))
mtb.plot.bubble(pd.concat(runs))

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
A dataset folder holds one file per role: a role is the name of one input, such as rna, atac_gas or cty, the label file. Dataset folder layout lists the file names, and mtb.scan(dataset, category) says which methods can run on a folder, and why not the rest.

mtb.method_info("SCALEX")["supports"][0]["modalities"]   # ['rna', 'atac_gas']
mtb.scan("D28", "diagonal")
Details

Each entry of supports is one variant: the version of a method for one category and one set of roles. For a method with several variants, run runs the one with the most of the folder's modalities. modalities=["rna", "adt"] picks another.

scan checks that each file is there and that no matrix is transposed. It also checks that each label file has as many rows as its matrix, and that files that must hold the same cells do. Its reason column names what is wrong.

docs.title: Dataset folder layout
docs.text:
Put the files of one dataset in one folder, <data_path>/<DATASET>/, for example data/MYDATA/. The folder name is the dataset name. mtb.io.export_dataset writes the folder from an AnnData or MuData.

Category Files vertical rna.h5 with adt.h5, atac.h5 or both, from the same cells, and cty.csv diagonal rna.h5 and rna_cty.csv for the RNA cells, atac_peak.h5, atac_gas.h5 or both, and atac_cty.csv for the ATAC cells mosaic one file per batch and modality, numbered by batch (rna1.h5, rna2.h5, atac2.h5 ...), and one label file per batch (cty1.csv, cty2.csv ...) cross as mosaic, with atac_peak1.h5, atac_peak2.h5 ... for ATAC

Each .h5 file holds matrix/data (features x cells, the transpose of AnnData.X), matrix/features and matrix/barcodes. R's rhdf5 shows the dimensions reversed, so write a cells x features matrix from R. A label file is a one-column CSV: a header line, then one label per cell, in the order of the cells.

Vertical, mosaic and cross methods read ATAC as peaks. In diagonal, atac_peak.h5 holds peaks and atac_gas.h5 gene-activity scores of the same cells, and each method reads one of them or both:

For several RNA and several ATAC batches in diagonal, scJoint, GLUE, iNMF and online_iNMF read exactly 3 of each. They are numbered rna1.h5, atac_gas1.h5 or atac_peak1.h5, rna_cty1.csv and atac_cty1.csv, then 2 and 3. For another number of batches, see Another number of donors.

docs.title: Your own data as a dataset folder
docs.text:
mtb.io.export_dataset writes an AnnData or MuData as a dataset folder, which scan and run read.

For a Cell Ranger .h5 file, labels in a CSV file, data without labels or another number of donors, see Recipes for your own data.

Give raw counts for RNA, ADT and peaks. The methods normalise the data themselves. The folder stores each matrix dense, so drop genes or peaks you do not need first.

With ATAC, set atac_kind= to "peak" or "gene_activity". Most methods read one of the two, and method_info(m)["atac"] names it. MultiMAP and Seurat_v3 read both. scan and run skip a method whose file holds the other one, also when methods= names it.

For CITE-seq, section 5 of the RNA + ADT tutorial writes the folder. Other layouts:

10x Multiome (MuData)Unpaired RNA + ATACOne file per batch 
import mudata as md      # pip install mudata

mdata = md.read_h5mu("my_multiome.h5mu")
# labels in mdata.obs; use rna:celltype for mdata["rna"].obs
mtb.io.export_dataset(mdata, "data/MYMULTIOME", rna="rna", atac="atac",
                      atac_kind="peak", labels="obs:celltype",
                      category="vertical")
mtb.scan("data/MYMULTIOME", "vertical", modalities=["rna", "atac"])
# on Linux or Windows: the RNA + ATAC methods; batch = each cell's sample
res = mtb.run("data/MYMULTIOME", "vertical", out_dir="out/",
              modalities=["rna", "atac_peak"], batch=mdata.obs["sample"])

Keep all samples in one folder and pass each cell's sample as batch=. atac_peak keeps the methods that read RNA and ATAC peaks.

import anndata as ad

rna = ad.read_h5ad("lung_rna.h5ad")
atac = ad.read_h5ad("lung_atac.h5ad")     # other cells than rna
mtb.io.export_dataset(rna, "data/LUNG", atac=atac, atac_kind="peak",
                      labels="obs:cell_type", category="diagonal")
peak_methods = mtb.find_methods("diagonal", modalities=["atac_peak"])
mtb.scan("data/LUNG", "diagonal", methods=peak_methods)

scan checks the four methods that read peaks. With peaks alone, only GLUE passes the file check. To add gene activity, see My ATAC is peaks only.

A mosaic or cross dataset can arrive as one file per batch. Here cite, multiome and rna_only hold one batch each.

kw = dict(labels="obs:cell_type", category="mosaic")
mtb.io.export_dataset(cite, "data/LAB", adt="obsm:protein",
                      batch_index=1, **kw)
mtb.io.export_dataset(multiome, "data/LAB", rna="rna", atac="atac",
                      atac_kind="peak", batch_index=2, **kw)
mtb.io.export_dataset(rna_only, "data/LAB", batch_index=3, **kw)
mtb.scan("data/LAB", "mosaic")

batch_index=N writes the whole object as batch N. Number the batches to match a pattern the methods read, as Dataset folder layout lists them. For cross, write each donor file the same way with category="cross". One file with a donor column is split by batch=:

mtb.io.export_dataset(adata, "data/MYCITE3", adt="obsm:protein",
                      labels="obs:celltype", batch="obs:donor",
                      category="cross")

The cross methods for RNA + ADT read batches 1-3. Dataset folder layout lists every batch pattern.

Details: files and labels

mtb.io.read reads a file of the folder back as an AnnData.

A label file is a one-column CSV: a header line x, then one label per cell, for example pd.Series(labels, name="x").to_csv(path, index=False).

A 10x Multiome AnnData read with gex_only=False holds genes and peaks in one X. Select each part with a feature filter: rna="X[feature_types=Gene Expression]" and atac="X[feature_types=Peaks]". Without a filter on such data, export_dataset raises ValueError. The recipe A 10x .h5 file reads the file and splits it.

Running an export again raises FileExistsError for the files already in the folder. overwrite=True replaces them. A call that fails writes nothing. An export also raises FileExistsError when the folder holds files of other data that it does not write: files with other cells, and after batch= files of other batch numbers. With batch_index=, a call checks its own batch number. The message names the first file. overwrite=True does not remove them. Write data with fewer batches into a new folder.

mtb.scan checks the folder for each method. Its caveat column flags values that are not whole numbers. When an expected file is missing, scan names the file it found instead.

Details: ATAC

The ATAC file name depends on the category. Vertical reads atac.h5. method_info(m)["atac"] names the form a method reads. Diagonal reads atac_peak.h5 for peaks and atac_gas.h5 for gene activity. Mosaic reads atac<i>.h5. The older name atac.h5 for gene activity still works.

GLUE and Seurat_v3 read peak names such as chr1:100-200. scan and run also skip these two methods when the peak names cannot be rewritten in that form, such as peak_0. With such names, scan cannot tell peaks from gene activity. The other methods run, with a caveat that names the file. scBridge reads the whole folder, and scan does not check its ATAC file. For a method skipped for its ATAC file, export the ATAC form it reads.

docs.title: Recipes for your own data
docs.text: Each task tutorial has a section "Your own data". It reads .h5ad files that hold the cell types in obs, writes a dataset folder and runs the methods on it. These recipes cover four other starting points. Run them in the tutorial notebook of your task. There mtb is imported, and METHODS is the list of methods from its section 2. Its check cell and run cell use NAME, the folder name that a recipe sets. The recipes write to mydata/ and call the cell-type column celltype, as the tutorials do.

docs.title: A 10x .h5 file
docs.text:
Cell Ranger writes filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5. One file holds one sample of cells measured in two modalities, which is the data of a vertical task. scan and run do not read this file. Read it with scanpy first.

import scanpy as sc

adata = sc.read_10x_h5("filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5",   # <- your file
                       gex_only=False)
print(adata.var["feature_types"].value_counts())

gex_only=False keeps the peaks or the antibody counts. Without it, scanpy returns the genes alone. The printout lists the feature types of the file. A 10x Multiome file holds Gene Expression and Peaks, and a CITE-seq file holds Gene Expression and Antibody Capture.

scanpy warns that variable names are not unique, here and in the next steps. Do not call var_names_make_unique on adata: on the whole object it also renames an antibody that has the name of a gene. The split below calls it on the genes only.

The file holds no cell types. Add them to adata now, before the split, with the blocks of Labels in a CSV file, on adata whatever the tutorial, then come back here for the split. Without cell types, leave the labels= line out of the export below, as in No labels.

Split adata into one AnnData per modality and write the folder. For 10x Multiome, in the vertical RNA + ATAC tutorial:

kind = adata.var["feature_types"]
rna = adata[:, kind == "Gene Expression"].copy()
rna.var_names_make_unique()     # the gene names only
atac = adata[:, kind == "Peaks"].copy()

NAME = "MY10X"   # <- a name for your data
mtb.io.export_dataset(rna, "mydata/" + NAME,
                      rna="X",
                      atac=atac,
                      atac_kind="peak",
                      labels="obs:celltype",
                      overwrite=True)

For CITE-seq, in the vertical RNA + ADT tutorial:

kind = adata.var["feature_types"]
rna = adata[:, kind == "Gene Expression"].copy()
rna.var_names_make_unique()     # the gene names only
adt = adata[:, kind == "Antibody Capture"].copy()

NAME = "MY10X"   # <- a name for your data
mtb.io.export_dataset(rna, "mydata/" + NAME,
                      rna="X",
                      adt=adt,
                      labels="obs:celltype",
                      overwrite=True)

When export_dataset says that a matrix holds 0 features, compare the type name in the split with the feature types printed above. A type that is not printed is not in adata: read the file again with gex_only=False.

Then run the check cell and the run cell of that tutorial. They use NAME, so they work on this folder:

mtb.scan("mydata/" + NAME, "vertical", methods=METHODS)

For 10x Multiome the check lists atac.h5 and atac_peak.h5: one matrix under two names, one copy on disk.

Each matrix is stored dense and read dense: features × cells × 8 bytes of memory. 150,000 peaks and 10,000 cells take 12 GB. Keep the genes and peaks you need before the export. export_dataset raises ValueError when a modality would hold two feature types, for example rna="X" on the object before the split.

docs.title: Labels in a CSV file
docs.text:
export_dataset reads the cell types from obs, not from a file. Read the CSV with pandas and add the column. The barcodes in the CSV must be unique: a duplicated barcode stops the block with the pandas error cannot reindex on an axis with duplicate labels. For diagonal data, do the recipe once for rna and once for atac.

In the code, adata is the object that holds your cells. In a tutorial that reads one object, it is adata. In the RNA + ATAC tutorials it is rna, and the name adata does not exist there: write rna for adata in every line of this recipe. With another name, such as adt or rna1, write the object whose cells the CSV lists.

import pandas as pd

ann = pd.read_csv("annotation.csv", index_col=0)               # <- your file, barcodes first
lab = ann["cluster_annotation"].astype(str).str.strip()        # <- your column
adata.obs["celltype"] = lab.where(~lab.isin(["", "NA", "nan"]))
print(adata.obs["celltype"].notna().sum(), "of", adata.n_obs, "cells have a label")

pandas matches the rows by barcode, so the CSV may be in any order. The third line turns a blank label and the text NA into a missing value, because a label file reads them as missing. When export_dataset names another such text, add it to that list.

The last line counts the cells that got a label. When it prints 0, or fewer cells than you expect, stop here. Some barcodes of the CSV are then spelled differently from adata.obs_names, often by an ending such as -1. Compare ann.index[:3] with adata.obs_names[:3], and do not go on until the number is right.

When the barcodes of the CSV lack the -1 ending that the cell names have, put the next line into the block above, after the line that reads the CSV, and run the block again. The line that reads the CSV comes first, so that a second run does not add the ending twice.

ann.index = ann.index + "-1"

A cell without a label cannot be scored, and export_dataset refuses it. When some cells have no label, keep the labelled cells.

adata = adata[adata.obs["celltype"].notna()].copy()

A second object of the same cells, such as atac, needs the same cells: atac = atac[adata.obs_names].copy(). Then go on with the export cell and labels="obs:celltype".

docs.title: No labels
docs.text:
Cell types are used for the scores. A few methods also read them as an input. The check names those methods: their reason says cty.csv is missing. The label file that it names depends on the layout. For diagonal data it is rna_cty.csv, for some methods together with atac_cty.csv: the reason then holds rna_cty.csv is missing. or rna_cty.csv, atac_cty.csv are missing. Without cell types, leave labels= out of the export and pass evaluate=False to run.

The two blocks below are those of the vertical RNA + ADT tutorial. In another tutorial, do the same by removing the labels= line of that tutorial's export cell, and pass evaluate=False in its run cell.

NAME = "MYDATA"   # <- a name for your data
mtb.io.export_dataset(adata, "mydata/" + NAME,
                      rna="X",              # <- where the RNA counts are
                      adt="obsm:protein",   # <- where the proteins (ADT) are
                      overwrite=True)
mtb.scan("mydata/" + NAME, "vertical", methods=METHODS)

mine = mtb.run("mydata/" + NAME, "vertical", methods=METHODS,
               out_dir="out/" + NAME, evaluate=False)
mine.summary[["method", "status"]]

The status ran means that the method ran and nothing was scored. skipped marks a method that needs cell types as an input. Each method that ran has a folder in out/MYDATA/. For most methods the embedding is the file embedding.h5 in it. Without evaluate=False the methods run as well, and the status ran says that nothing was scored.

Diagonal data with cell types for the RNA cells only is the same case. run scores a diagonal folder only when both sides have labels. Leave labels= out and pass evaluate=False. No score compares methods on such data: scores of the RNA cells alone do not change with where a method puts the ATAC cells.

When you have cell types later, add them to the folder and score the saved embeddings. No method runs again. Here adata is the object whose cells the folder holds. In the vertical RNA + ATAC tutorial it is rna.

mtb.io.export_dataset(adata, "mydata/" + NAME, rna=None, labels="obs:celltype",
                      overwrite=True)
mine = mtb.load_run("out/" + NAME).rescore()
mine.save()                        # the new scores into out/MYDATA
mine.summary

export_dataset writes the labels in the cell order of the files already in the folder, whatever the row order of adata is by then. It refuses labels for other cells.

This line is for a folder without batch numbers that holds one set of cells, as the vertical tutorials write it. For cross, mosaic and diagonal data it does not apply: run the export cell of your tutorial again with its labels= line, and then the rescore line above. The files keep their cell order. Diagonal data needs the column in both files.

With cell types for some of the cells only, keep the labelled cells before the export, as in the recipe above. evaluate raises when a label is missing: score an embedding on its labelled cells, as mtb.evaluate(emb[emb.obs["label"].notna()], labels="label").

docs.title: Another number of donors
docs.text:
A batch is a donor, a sample or an experiment. A cross method reads a fixed number of batches: three for RNA + ADT and for RNA + ATAC, and two for ADT + ATAC and for RNA + ADT + ATAC. Dataset folder layout lists them. With another number of donors, treat the data as a vertical task: keep all cells in one folder and give run the donor of each cell.

Do this in the vertical tutorial of your modalities. Its METHODS are vertical methods, and its section 2 installs their environments. ADT + ATAC has no vertical task: for that data, keep two donors, as shown further down, with two names in the list.

NAME = "MYDONORS"   # <- a name for your data
mtb.io.export_dataset(adata, "mydata/" + NAME,
                      rna="X",                # <- where the RNA counts are
                      adt="obsm:protein",     # <- where the proteins (ADT) are
                      labels="obs:celltype",  # <- the cell-type column
                      overwrite=True)         # no batch= here
mine = mtb.run("mydata/" + NAME, "vertical", methods=METHODS,
               out_dir="out/" + NAME,
               batch=adata.obs["donor"])  # <- your donor column
mine.summary

The methods do not read batch=. The summary then has the batch metrics ASW_batch, ARI_batch, NMI_batch, GC and iLISI, which say how well the donors mix. batch= takes the column itself, not its name. run reads the folder, and the folder holds no obs columns. The values are matched to the cells by barcode. Every cell needs a donor: run stops when one is missing.

For diagonal data with another number of donors than 3, do the same in the diagonal RNA + ATAC tutorial. Export rna and atac with all their cells, without batch_index=, and give run the donor of every RNA and ATAC cell:

import pandas as pd

mine = mtb.run("mydata/" + NAME, "diagonal", methods=METHODS,
               out_dir="out/" + NAME,
               batch=pd.concat([rna.obs["donor"], atac.obs["donor"]]))  # <- your column

To use the cross tutorial instead, keep as many donors as its methods read. First print the donor names of your file. This block changes nothing.

print(adata.obs["donor"].value_counts())   # the names in your file

Write as many of the printed names as the methods read into the list of the next block, in place of A, B and C. Then run it.

adata = adata[adata.obs["donor"].isin(["A", "B", "C"])].copy()   # <- the donors to keep

When none of the names is in the file, no cell is kept, and the export stops: The data holds 0 cells, so there is nothing to write. When one name is wrong, the cells of the other donors are kept, and the check names the files of the batch that is not there.

When the list holds a name that is not in the file, adata ends with fewer cells or with none, and a corrected list does not bring them back. Run the read cell of the tutorial again to get the data back, and then this block.

In a cross folder with more batches than a method reads, the method reads the first ones, and the check says so: StabMap reads batches 1-3 of 5. Batches 4-5 are not used. With fewer, it names the files that are not there: rna3.h5, adt3.h5 are missing. The batches are numbered in the sorted order of the donor names, read as text, so 10 comes before 2.

docs.title: GPU or CPU?
docs.text:
Most methods also run without a GPU, only slower. Six need an NVIDIA GPU. On a host without one, scan and run mark them not runnable.

[m for m in mtb.find_methods() if mtb.method_info(m)["gpu"] == "required"]
# ['scBridge', 'moETM', 'SMILE', 'sciCAN', 'UnitedNet', 'iPOLNG']
mtb.method_info("scJoint")["cpu_params"]
# {'use_cuda': ''}
Details

scJoint and scMDC use CUDA unless told otherwise. On a host without a GPU, run adds the flags in method_info(m)["cpu_params"] and prints one line to stderr. A key you pass in params wins.

Six torch environments, env_sciPENN, matilda, scmb_scjoint, scmb_torch, scmb_scmm2 and scmb_multigrate2, also come as smaller CPU-only builds. mtb.env.install picks them on a host without a GPU, and flavor="cpu" or "gpu" overrides that. scMM never uses a GPU, so scmb_scmm2 comes as its CPU build on every host. Both builds install under the environment's own name, and the flavor column of mtb.env.install(..., dry_run=True) reports the installed one.

Next: score an embedding of your own, then draw the bubble table.

docs.title: Vertical integration: RNA + ADT¶
docs.text:
Vertical integration combines modalities measured in the same cells. This tutorial is for RNA and surface protein, as in CITE-seq. It runs Matilda and sciPENN on D11, a CITE-seq dataset of 2,864 cells, and then on data in your own format.

Methods run on Linux. On macOS or Windows, open this notebook in Colab: sections 1 to 4 take about 7 minutes there.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text: pip may then print a note about restarting the kernel: no restart is needed, because the pins keep the numpy and pandas already installed.

docs.title: 2. Download the data and the environments¶
docs.text: mtb.data.fetch downloads D11 (11 MB) once. mtb.env.install downloads the environments for Matilda and sciPENN. The download is 1.1 GB on a computer without a GPU and 5.1 GB on one with a GPU.

docs.title: 3. Run the methods¶
docs.text:
run runs each method on D11 and scores its output with the scIB metrics. The clustering metrics score how well the embedding's clusters and neighbourhoods match the cell types, and how separate the clusters are. Higher is better for every metric.

Details

params={"Method": {"key": value}} sets a method's parameters, and mtb.params_for lists them.

mtb.load_run("out/D11") reloads these results later.

docs.title: 4. Plot¶
docs.text:
res.plot() draws the scores as a bubble table. Circle size ranks the rows within each column and colour shows the value scaled per column, so a small gap can look large. res.summary has the values.

Details

Metrics are grouped by family: blue for clustering. Each family starts with an Overall bar: each row's mean rank over the family's metrics, scaled so that the lowest gets the shortest bar.

A column with fewer than two different values is drawn grey. A figure of one method is grey everywhere.

docs.title: 5. Your own data¶
docs.text:
Your data needs raw counts for both modalities and a cell type for each cell, in one .h5ad file.

Recipes cover a 10x .h5 file, labels in a CSV file, no labels and several donors or samples.

Details: export

The example keeps the protein names in adata.uns["protein_names"]. A DataFrame in adata.obsm["protein"] brings its own names in its columns.

docs.title: 6. Stored results¶
docs.text:
The package ships stored results for 13 methods on D11. load_results reads them and mtb.plot.bubble draws them, without running anything.

Details

docs.text:
Vertical integration combines modalities measured in the same cells. This tutorial is for RNA, surface protein and ATAC from the same cells. It runs Matilda and UINMF on D22mini, 3,000 cells of the benchmark dataset D22, and then on data in your own format.

Methods run on Linux. On macOS or Windows, open this notebook in Colab: sections 1 to 4 take about 6 minutes there.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text: pip may then print a note about restarting the kernel: no restart is needed, because the pins keep the numpy and pandas already installed.

docs.title: 2. Download the data and the environments¶
docs.text: mtb.data.fetch downloads D22mini (8 MB) once. mtb.env.install downloads the environments for Matilda and UINMF. The download is 1.5 GB on a computer without a GPU and 4.0 GB on one with a GPU.

docs.title: 3. Run the methods¶
docs.text:
run runs each method on D22mini and scores its output with the scIB metrics. The clustering metrics score how well the embedding's clusters and neighbourhoods match the cell types, and how separate the clusters are. Higher is better for every metric.

Details

params={"Method": {"key": value}} sets a method's parameters, and mtb.params_for lists them.

mtb.load_run("out/D22mini") reloads these results later.

docs.title: 4. Plot¶
docs.text:
res.plot() draws the scores as a bubble table. Circle size ranks the rows within each column and colour shows the value scaled per column, so a small gap can look large. res.summary has the values.

Details

Metrics are grouped by family: blue for clustering. Each family starts with an Overall bar: each row's mean rank over the family's metrics, scaled so that the lowest gets the shortest bar.

A column with fewer than two different values is drawn grey. A figure of one method is grey everywhere.
